headline: AI consulting's core incentive problem: vendors optimize for dependency, not client graduation
summary: A $7.7 billion AI-driven take-private deal highlights a core problem: consultants are paid to stay, not to reinvent your business. This incentive structure applies at every budget level.
details: A $7.7 billion deal to take insurance broker Baldwin private by Sequence Holdings and Michael Dell's family office has put the AI-consulting business model on trial. This is the largest AI-driven take-private to date, with Sequence's model involving embedding its own engineers permanently within acquired companies.

Sequence CEO Michael Lee explained the diagnosis: "Consultants are paid to stay, and software is sold to the workflow as it exists today." This highlights that services firms optimize to keep you as a customer, not to fundamentally reinvent your business.

The incentive problem in AI consulting is not theoretical; it's openly discussed by those funding these deals. The pattern is subtle because each step feels reasonable, but a services business grows by retaining clients, and a client who has "graduated" no longer pays a retainer.

To use consultants effectively, hire for a defined outcome with a built-in ending. Structure for handover from day one, agreeing on what "done" looks like and who owns it afterward, including documentation and training. If a proposal lacks a handover plan, ask for one.

Prefer fixed-scope for implementation projects like "Build and wire up our invoice-exception automation for $X, including a runbook and one training session." Avoid retainers for "Manage your AI," which can create a subscription to dependency. Fixed-scope aligns incentives towards completion and handover.

Always own your accounts: set up API keys, subscriptions, and platforms under your business email, even if the consultant configures them. If these are in their account, it's their leverage, not your capability. Treat the runbook, documenting how automation works, as the actual product.

Consider the "celebrated persona" test: a company's celebrated persona dictates who it hires. A consulting firm whose stars are salespeople will staff your account with handoffs, while one whose stars are engineers embeds capability. Ask if the person doing the work aims to become unnecessary.

The counterpoint: embedded engineers at a holding company transformed BankSouth's commercial loan process, reducing it from 30 days to 11 with 94% less consumer underwriting in six months. This demonstrates that transformation compounds when capability resides within your organization.

The lesson isn't to never hire outside help, but that capability should end up inside your walls, not rented. The AI consulting wave has an incentive problem where the vendor's best month is when you never graduate. Structure for the opposite: fix the outcome, fix the ending, own the accounts, and pay for the handover.

headline_marked: [[Google Messages to remove 'send SMS only' toggle]], forcing RCS for all contacts
headline: Google Messages to remove 'send SMS only' toggle, forcing RCS for all contacts
summary: An APK teardown suggests Google Messages will soon remove the option to disable RCS for individual contacts, limiting user control and potentially increasing spam.
details: An APK teardown of a Google Messages beta version (messages.android_20261002_00_RC00.phone.openbeta_dynamic) indicates Google is preparing to remove a key RCS feature.
Currently, users can find a toggle labeled "Only send SMS and MMS messages" within a conversation's details screen. This allows forcing SMS/MMS for specific contacts instead of RCS.
With its removal, users will face a choice: either disable RCS entirely across the app or keep it enabled for every contact. This eliminates granular control over messaging protocols.
Leaked code strings reveal a banner notification that will warn users about the impending change, prompting them to "Switch to RCS chats now" or let it update automatically.
The exact timeline for this removal is not specified in the code, but its presence in a beta version suggests it could be implemented relatively soon.
Critics argue this move is detrimental as it reduces user choice and removes an effective method for preventing spam within Google Messages conversations.
caption:
